sharedText: come unto me and be ye baptized
reason: A cross-reference, not a rejection (PLAN §3, ruled 2026-09-07). The machine ranked Isaiah 45:22 here on 'unto me and be ye', and the contact is real: the Lord's command to Mormon — 'repent ye, and come unto me and be ye baptized' — is the first half of a formula whose second half arrives at the end of the chapter, 'all ye ends of the earth to repent' (3:22). The Book of Mormon has both halves in one sentence at 3 Nephi 27:20, in the record Mormon abridged, and Isaiah 45:22 stands behind that. The link is therefore adjudicated at 3:22, where the vocative that carries it actually appears, and a reader who arrives at 3:2 should be sent there. Note also that 'and be ye baptized' occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses; nothing in this half of the formula is King James English.

This one has to be written out because the rarity count looks decisive and is not. 'Harden their hearts' occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Joshua 11:20, 'For it was of the LORD to harden their hearts, that they should come against Israel in battle, that he might destroy them utterly' — and the context is a startlingly good fit for Mormon 3, where hardened hearts (3:3) produce a march to battle (3:10) and end in being cut off from the face of the earth (3:15). The count is nevertheless worthless here, because the phrase is one of the Book of Mormon's most heavily worn formulas: it occurs in thirty-five verses spread across every book from 1 Nephi to Ether. A formula used thirty-five times cannot be evidence of dependence on the one KJV verse that happens to share it. The agency also differs at the point that matters: in Joshua it is the LORD who hardens, in Mormon 3:3 the people harden their own hearts against him. Filed as the model case for a KJV singleton that a Book of Mormon commonplace has neutralised.

sharedText: that they should gather themselves together
reason: The chapter's highest-scoring machine candidate, a six-word run, and pure formula. Ezra 10:7 proclaims that the children of the captivity 'should gather themselves together unto Jerusalem' for a covenant assembly; Mormon 3:5 musters an army at the land Desolation to hold a narrow pass. 'Gather themselves together' is the King James Bible's standing phrase for any assembly of people, and the Book of Mormon uses it continuously in exactly this military sense throughout the war narratives. Nothing else of Ezra 10 is present.

'Then Philip went down to the city of Samaria, and preached Christ unto them' against 'the Lamanites did come down to the city of Desolation to battle'. The shared string is a preposition, a direction and the ordinary way of naming a city in English. Covered by the standing formulaic exclusion; listed only because it ranked in the chapter's top twenty-four.

'Utterly refuse' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and a reader who runs the count will find it: Exodus 22:17, 'If her father utterly refuse to give her unto him, he shall pay money according to the dowry of virgins' — the seducer's fine in the covenant code. Mormon uses the phrase twice in six verses (3:11, 3:16), which is the only place in the Book of Mormon it occurs, so the rarity is real at both ends. The senses have nothing whatever in common. Exodus 22:17 is a father withholding a daughter from a marriage and being compensated in silver; Mormon 3:11 is a general resigning a command. The adverb is the KJV's ordinary intensifier for a refusal and would be reached for by anyone writing in that register. Recorded at length because the double singleton is exactly the shape of evidence this catalogue accepts elsewhere, and here it means nothing.

The same trap as the Joshua 11:20 entry at 3:3, one verse of the King James Bible and seventeen of the Book of Mormon. 'Hardness of their hearts' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 3:5, where Jesus is grieved at it in the synagogue before healing the withered hand; it occurs in seventeen Book of Mormon verses from 1 Nephi 2:18 onward, as the book's standing explanation for any failure of preaching. Mormon 3:12 is one of the seventeen. The catalogue does hold a Mark 3:5 link — at 1 Nephi 17:53, for 'stretch forth thine hand', which is the half of the verse a formula has not swallowed.

Tempting and declined. 'Poured out my soul' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hannah's answer to Eli at 1 Samuel 1:15 — a woman of a sorrowful spirit pouring out her soul before the LORD and taken for a drunkard. Mormon 3:12 reads 'my soul had been poured out in prayer unto my God all the day long', and the situation rhymes: unavailing prayer, misread by the people it is offered for. But the Book of Mormon's clause is passive where Hannah's is active, the possessive differs, and the book pours out souls elsewhere without any Samuel vocabulary (Alma 46:17, Mosiah 26:14). What is left is a shared metaphor that the Psalms use too (42:4, 62:8). The love-of-God clause is where this verse's link is; see the Romans 8:39 row.

The machine's only candidate at the chapter's most important verse, and it is boilerplate sitting next to a certain quotation. 'Cut off' is the covenant code's standing penalty formula and the Book of Mormon's standing threat; Leviticus 20:17 is a prohibited-degrees law about a man and his sister. The verse's actual borrowing is the clause before it, 'Vengeance is mine, and I will repay', adjudicated as a quotation of Romans 12:19. Recorded so that a reader who sees only the machine's proposal at 3:15 knows the catalogue looked past it.

sharedText: unto all the ends of the earth
reason: A seven-word run and the longest in the chapter, which is what got it ranked. 'All the ends of the earth' occurs in exactly seven KJV verses (Psalm 65:5, 67:7, 98:3, Proverbs 30:4, Isaiah 26:15, 45:22, 52:10) and in twenty-three Book of Mormon verses, eight of which carry it as the vocative 'all ye ends of the earth'. Isaiah 26:15 is about the enlargement of the nation and has nothing else in common with a passage about two benches of twelve judges. The one Isaiah verse of the seven that does bear on this chapter is 45:22, and it is adjudicated at 3:22, where the imperative that identifies it appears.

A four-word run, and 'according to their works' occurs in exactly three KJV verses (2 Corinthians 11:15, Revelation 20:12, 20:13) with Revelation 2:23's second-person variant beside them — a genuinely rare formula, and one the Book of Mormon has already fixed for itself. 3 Nephi 27:15, in the record Mormon abridged, has the risen Christ say men shall 'be judged according to their works', and Mormon 6:21 repeats the phrase with the judgement seat attached. The judgment-of-works material in this chapter is adjudicated at 3:20, where the whole composite stands (2 Corinthians 5:10, Romans 14:10, Ecclesiastes 12:14); the Apocalypse is not needed for it and nothing else of Revelation 2 or 20 is present.

'The gospel of Jesus Christ' at Mark 1:1 against 'the Gospel of Jesus Christ, which ye shall have among you'. The phrase is the New Testament's ordinary name for the thing and the Book of Mormon's too, and Mark 1:1 contributes nothing else. The verse's real borrowings are two clauses later — 'whom they slew' and 'the very Christ' — and both are adjudicated.
